conceptTag: Tesla started with an expensive sports car
readerTitle: Why Tesla's first car was one most people couldn't afford
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Tesla, Roadster → Model S → Model 3) + 가상 적용 (동결건조 식품 스타트업, softwareNote의 AI 도구)
insight: 새 기술이 처음에 비싸다면 대중 시장이 아니라 비싼 값을 기꺼이 내는 소수에게 먼저 팔고, 그 돈과 경험으로 한 단계씩 내려온다.
misconception: 큰 시장을 노리려면 처음부터 싸고 대중적인 제품으로 시작해야 한다.

sources.text: Elon Musk, "The Secret Tesla Motors Master Plan (just between you and me)", Tesla blog, August 2006
Tesla Roadster: Lotus Elise 기반 차체, 2008년 출고 시작, 약 $100,000 수준 가격 (Tesla 보도자료 및 당시 주요 언론 보도)
Model S 출고 2012년, Model 3 출고 2017년·기본가 $35,000 발표 (Tesla 보도자료, 연례 보고서)
2008년 자금난과 Model 3 생산 지연 ('production hell'): Elon Musk 공개 발언 및 주요 언론 보도

factChecks.note: 2006년 마스터플랜 블로그 글의 요지(스포츠카 → 그 돈으로 더 싼 차 → 그 돈으로 더 싼 차)는 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 직접 인용 대신 요약으로 적었습니다.
Roadster 가격은 트림과 연도에 따라 약 $98,000~$109,000으로 보도됩니다. 카드에는 "about $100,000"로만 적었습니다.
Roadster 총 생산 대수는 약 2,450대로 자주 인용되지만 자료마다 다릅니다. 카드에는 "a few thousand"로만 적었습니다.
Roadster가 Lotus Elise 차체를 바탕으로 만들어졌다는 점, 2008년 말 회사가 파산 직전까지 갔다는 점, Model 3 출고 시작(2017년)과 $35,000 기본가 발표를 게시 전 다시 확인하세요.
"당시 전기차는 작고 느리고 밋밋하다는 인식이 있었다"는 일반적 서술입니다. 특정 차종이나 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why Tesla's first car was one most people couldn't afford
body: In 2006, a small startup wanted to put electric cars on every street.
Its first product was a two-seat sports car that sold for about $100,000. On paper, that looks like the wrong way to reach everyone.

image.label: A sleek two-seat electric sports car on an empty road
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 낮고 날렵한 2인승 전기 스포츠카 한 대가 빈 도로 위에 있고, 뒤로 멀리 평범한 가족용 차들이 줄지어 기다리는 실루엣. 실제 Tesla 로고, 엠블럼, 차량 디자인은 그대로 쓰지 말 것.

cards.title: Batteries are expensive. What do you build first?
body: It's 2006. You run a young electric car company. Batteries cost a lot, and you can only build a small number of cars. Many people think electric cars are small, slow and dull.
Your goal is affordable electric cars for millions. What should your first car be?

options.text: An affordable family car, so you reach the big market right away
options.feedback: You aim straight at the goal, but at low volume each car costs far more than families will pay. You'd lose money on every sale.

options.text: An expensive, fast sports car for wealthy car lovers
options.feedback: A few buyers pay a price that can cover high early costs, and a fast car fights the 'slow and dull' image. The trade-off: you start with a tiny market.

options.text: A cheap, small city car for short trips
options.feedback: Smaller batteries keep costs down. But it confirms the image you need to break, and cheap prices leave little to fund what comes next.

cards.title: A sports car, with a plan written down.
body: Tesla's first car, the Roadster, was built on the frame of a Lotus sports car and began reaching buyers in 2008. Only a few thousand were ever made.

In 2006, before it shipped, Elon Musk posted what he called the company's *master plan*. In short: build a sports car, use that money to build a more affordable car, then use that money to build an even more affordable one.
The expensive car wasn't a detour from the mass market. It was the **first step toward it**.

cards.title: Enter at the top, then move down
body: **Top-down entry** means launching a new technology first to the small group who will pay the most for it, then lowering the price step by step as costs fall.
It works because early units are expensive to make. A high price covers those costs. Each step builds money, skill and volume that make the next, cheaper step possible.
It also shapes what people think the product *is*. Tesla's first car said electric could mean fast.
cards.softwareNote: A new AI tool may cost a lot to run per customer at first. Selling it to law firms or engineers who save hours with it can fund the work that later makes a cheaper self-serve plan possible.

cards.title: Three steps down the price ladder.
body: Each car sold to a larger group than the one before. Prices still weren't cheap, but the direction was clear.

breakdown.label: Roadster
breakdown.detail: Two-seat sports car, about $100,000, a few thousand made

breakdown.label: Model S
breakdown.detail: Luxury sedan, still pricey, far more buyers

cards.callout: The goal stayed the same. Only the starting point was unusual.

cards.title: "Go where the volume is" isn't always right.
body: Common launch advice says to pick the biggest market you can. For a product whose costs are high at small scale, that can be a trap. You chase buyers who won't pay what each unit costs.
The better question is: *who will pay enough today for the product I can actually make today?* Sometimes that's a large group. For new, costly technology, it's often a small, demanding one.

cards.title: The ladder only works if you survive each step.
body: Top-down entry needs costs to fall as volume grows. If they don't, you stay a niche luxury maker.
It's also risky. Tesla reportedly came close to running out of money in late 2008, and Musk later described the Model 3 ramp-up as "production hell."
And a premium image can be hard to move down. Early fans may not want their special product to become common.

cards.title: Now it's freeze-dried meals.
body: Your startup has a new way to freeze-dry restaurant-quality meals that taste fresh. In small batches, each meal costs $14 to make. At large scale, you expect that to fall a lot.
Who should you sell to first?

options.text: Supermarkets nationwide at $6 a meal, to grow fast
options.feedback: You'd reach many shoppers but lose about $8 a meal until scale arrives, and you might not last that long.

options.text: Mountaineers, sailors and expedition outfitters who pay well for great food far from kitchens
options.feedback: They value taste and weight enough to cover today's costs, and their praise builds credibility. You'll still need a plan for stepping down to wider markets.

options.text: A mid-priced online store at $12, to test general demand
options.feedback: You learn something about wider demand, but you still lose money per meal and blur what makes the product special.

cards.title: Start where people pay for what you can make today.
body: If your product is costly at small scale, a high-end first customer can fund the road to a mass market. The plan only works if costs fall and you last long enough to take each step.
**Try it today:** write down what one unit costs you now and at ten times the volume. Which customers would pay the first number?
